title: Nolan Wells Case: Grand Jury Decides No Criminal Charges
seoTitle: Nolan Wells Case: Grand Jury Decides No Criminal Charges
subtitle: Investigation found the 18‑year‑old died in a manner consistent with accidental drowning in Mississippi.
excerpt: The Jackson County grand jury concluded there was no crime or racial motive in the death of athlete Nolan Wells, determining it was an accidental drowning.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The Jackson County grand jury in the U.S. state of Mississippi unanimously decided not to bring criminal charges in the death of 18‑year‑old Nolan Wells. The investigation concluded there was no crime or racial motive in the case of the college football athlete, who disappeared after a trip to an island in July. The result was released after reviewing phone records, testimonies and forensic reports.

What Happened on Horn Island

Wells traveled to Horn Island, about 10 miles off the Mississippi coast, with a group of friends on July 4 to celebrate the holiday. He was found dead in the water on the morning of July 6. The youth had been aboard the vessel "The Triton," which experienced a bilge pump and engine failure on the return trip and had to be towed by another boat. However, the jury noted that Wells chose to stay on the island to keep socializing after the boats departed. His cell phone later returned to the mainland on a different vessel, as did the phones of other passengers.

Medical Findings and Cause of Death

Both the chief medical examiner of Mississippi and an independent forensic pathologist hired by Wells' family agreed that the cause and manner of death were indeterminate. Court documents indicate the death is consistent with accidental drowning, a possibility not ruled out by authorities. The body showed a non‑fatal bruise on the back of the head. A sworn witness stated that Wells slipped awkwardly on the side of a boat but continued socializing and did not appear injured. No fatal physical trauma was found, nor any cocaine in the toxicology report. The youth had purchased alcoholic drinks using a false ID, and no adult over 21 provided alcohol to the group.

Clarification on Rumors and Viral Images

The 23‑member grand jury examined forensic cell‑phone reports, GPS logs, security‑camera footage, 132 subpoenas and testimonies from 43 witnesses. The legal team hired by Wells' family also found no evidence of criminal activity to forward to prosecutors. Consequently, authorities debunked online rumors about an alleged fight involving Wells and accusations against his friends. Viral photos of the youth at a pool party were taken before July 4, and an audio clip purportedly from a SeaTow tow‑service call was inaccurate compared to the original recording. The rumor that the state morgue had retained organs pending an independent autopsy was also denied.

Possibility of Reopening the Investigation

District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath stated in a release that there is no evidence the death of the Black youth was racially motivated. She emphasized that Wells' friends loved him and that he chose to remain on the island. Although no one will be indicted, court documents remind that Mississippi has no statute of limitations for homicide. If credible new evidence of a crime emerges, the case could be reopened and presented to a new jury.

With information from WLOX, New York Post.
